planGoal: Bridge server-side operational alerts to desktop client via GET /alerts + POST /alerts/acknowledge endpoints, IPC handlers, and a 60-second polling hook

findings.step: Task 1A: GET /alerts and POST /alerts/acknowledge — no authentication
findings.description: The plan explicitly states 'These endpoints do NOT require authentication (they return no PII, only operational event_type/message/severity)'. However, the alert messages contain operational details that reveal server internals: account IDs (e.g., 'Sync failed for account abc-123 after 3 retries'), bank session IDs, aspsp names, and IP addresses (from auth_failure_burst: 'N authentication failures from IP x.x.x.x in Ys'). The IP address in auth_failure_burst messages is PII under GDPR. The endpoints are fully unauthenticated — any network actor that can reach the sync-server can enumerate these alerts.
findings.suggestion: Apply validateSessionMiddleware to both /alerts endpoints, matching the protection level of other sensitive routes. Remove IP addresses from alert messages (they are already in the audit_log; the alert message only needs the count and time window). Review all alert message templates in scheduler.ts and app-account.ts for embedded PII or sensitive identifiers.

findings.step: Task 1B: fetchOperationalAlerts — uses get() not post()
findings.description: The plan's interface section documents post() as 'POST with JSON body' but fetchOperationalAlerts() was implemented using get() (verified in provider-status.ts line 479). The plan's interface snippet shows `return post(serverConfig.BASE_SERVER + '/alerts', {}, ...)` but the actual code uses get(). The get() function in post.ts (line 217-219) returns raw text and does NOT send X-ACTUAL-TOKEN headers — it takes an `opts` object passed directly to fetch(). The implementation passes `{ headers: { 'X-ACTUAL-TOKEN': userToken } }` which goes into fetch's init, so the header IS sent correctly. However the plan's interface documentation for get() shows `get(url, opts?)` with `opts` as optional — no mention of headers support — making it easy to misuse.
findings.suggestion: The implementation is correct (get() passes opts to fetch). Update the plan's interface documentation to show get(url, opts?) supports standard fetch init options including headers.

findings.description: The knownAlertIds Set grows without bound across the component's lifetime. If a user leaves the app running for days and hundreds of alerts fire, acknowledged alerts are removed server-side but their IDs stay in knownAlertIds forever. The Set prevents re-displaying acknowledged alerts (correct), but acknowledged alerts with stable IDs can never reappear even if the server restarts (resetting alertCounter). After a server restart, new alerts get ids starting from alert-1 again, which may collide with already-acknowledged IDs in knownAlertIds, silently suppressing new alerts.
findings.suggestion: Clear knownAlertIds entries for acknowledged alerts (in the onClose callback, after the server acknowledge call succeeds). Or scope knownAlertIds to the server's session by including a server-generated nonce in the alert ID.

findings.step: Task 2: useOperationalAlerts — no deduplication with useConsentExpiryNotifications
findings.description: Both useConsentExpiryNotifications() and useOperationalAlerts() can fire notifications for consent expiry. useConsentExpiryNotifications reads from the Redux EB status state (polling enablebanking-sync-status). useOperationalAlerts() polls server-side alerts which include consent_expiry events from the scheduler. A user could see two separate notifications for the same consent expiry situation — one from the client-side check and one from the server-side alert — with different message text.
findings.suggestion: Either suppress consent_expiry events in useOperationalAlerts() (since useConsentExpiryNotifications already handles this from the client side), or remove the client-side consent expiry hook and rely solely on server-side alerts. Document the chosen boundary explicitly.

findings.step: Task 1A: POST /alerts/acknowledge — no authentication means anyone can acknowledge
findings.description: Beyond the information disclosure issue (finding 1), the lack of authentication on POST /alerts/acknowledge means any network actor can silently dismiss all operational alerts before the legitimate admin sees them. This creates a blind spot where an attacker performing a credential stuffing attack could clear the auth_failure_burst alerts to avoid detection.
findings.suggestion: Authenticate both /alerts endpoints. This is the same fix as finding 1 — validateSessionMiddleware resolves both the read and the write exposure.

findings.step: Task 1A: Endpoint placement — before route mounts
findings.description: The plan instructs adding /alerts endpoints 'BEFORE the route mounts (e.g., before app.use('/plaid', ...))'. Looking at the actual app.ts, there is no /plaid route. The instruction references a route that doesn't exist. This is a stale reference that could confuse an executor looking for the insertion point.
findings.suggestion: Reference existing routes for insertion context. The actual implementation placed the endpoints correctly after /metrics (verified in codebase). The stale /plaid reference is documentation debt.

missingSteps: No test coverage for the /alerts or /alerts/acknowledge endpoints — the sync-server test suite does not include integration tests for these new routes.
No cleanup of knownAlertIds on server restart detection (alertCounter reset causes ID collisions that silently suppress new alerts).
assumptions: Alert messages contain no PII — this is incorrect for auth_failure_burst (contains source IP) and sync_failure (contains internal account IDs). The plan's stated justification for unauthenticated endpoints does not hold.
Server restarts are infrequent enough that alertCounter ID collisions with knownAlertIds are not a practical concern.
The 60-second polling interval is acceptable latency for operational alerts reaching the user.
